title: Called as a Slave, Free in Christ
english: …at times, though they had received the faith, they were seeking to be made complete in the flesh, just as some in Galatia did, whom the inspired Paul rebukes, saying, “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being made complete in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3).

So the way had to be opened wide for them by a clear and most vivid proclamation of the truth: that circumcision is nothing when it lacks the other commandments of God, and in the same way uncircumcision is nothing unless it is adorned with a life worthy of the Gospel (compare 1 Corinthians 7:19). It is fitting, then, that the one who has been called should remain in his calling, in whatever state he may be (compare 1 Corinthians 7:20).

He then passes, of necessity, to the need to drive off once more, as it were, another slander against the divine proclamation. For there was a spirit of slavery in those under the law; but the decree of the Gospel says that the Spirit of adoption is given to those who are willing to believe, and that it no longer calls them to slavery but to the dignity of the free (compare Romans 8:15).
By the same Cyril, from the fourth tome of his work on the Epistle to the Corinthians.

“Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you” (1 Corinthians 7:21). Since some who had been counted worthy of the grace of the Holy Spirit were shaking off the yoke of slavery according to the flesh, he writes in another place too, “Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians 5:13). Here also he wins them over, as it were, speaking with great grace: “Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you; but even if you can become free, rather make use of it” (1 Corinthians 7:21).

That is: even if you were called through faith into free sonship while you still bore the yoke of slavery according to the flesh, even if you have become a partaker of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), rise above faint-heartedness; you will find that the toil you bear in slavery is not without its reward. For the Creator knows our nature as free, since it was made so by him; but a kind of greed, slipping in somehow over the course of time, has ruined the beauty of freedom.

Those who have suffered this must by all means throw off the burden of this evil, since Christ is refashioning all things to what they were in the beginning. For what is in him is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and there is neither slave nor free, but he himself is all and in all (Colossians 3:11). Indeed Isaiah cried out beforehand about the state of the life we await, the life that is to be, and about the equality that is found with God, saying, “And the people shall be as the priest, and the servant as his master, and the maidservant as her mistress” (Isaiah 24:2).

So, he says, even if you could become free, rather make use of it; for, as I said, the yoke is not without gain for those who have shown good will and have lived rightly under it. That slavery according to the flesh has now been laid on some out of greed will do no wrong at all, so long as freedom is kept for all alike, in equal manner and measure, before God, who judges what is just and weighs our affairs in holiness.

Besides, he says, since we are human beings, it is not possible for us to escape the name of slavery. For everything that has been made is a slave, and all that has been called into being is subject to the divine scepter. So the slave is Christ’s freedman, and the one called to freedom is surely a slave as well (compare 1 Corinthians 7:22), as the psalm says, “for all things are your slaves” (Psalm 119:91).

Yet the guide into the mysteries shows in another way too that those saved through Christ are helped by him. That is why he says, “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (1 Corinthians 7:23). For we were, beyond dispute, bought with a price, since Christ, the Savior of us all, paid his own blood for us; we have been rescued from the greed of the devil and from the cruelty of the demons, and we have been called to freedom through Christ (compare Galatians 5:13). So, as those who have been bought and who owe their own life to the One who purchased them, “do not become,” he says, “slaves of men.”
We do not say that he is urging them to leap out of slavery according to the flesh; rather he teaches this, and very rightly: not to be slaves to those who try to carry off…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Khazarzar transcription). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The section opens mid-sentence. The Greek ‘ἔσθ’ ὅτε’ (‘at times’) is split across the break: ‘ἔσθ’’ ends the previous section and ‘ὅτε’ begins this one. ‘At times’ is rendered here.

The section also ends mid-sentence (‘τοῖς ἀποφέρειν | τοὺς πεπιστευκότας ἐπιχειροῦσιν εἰς νομικὴν παρατήρησιν’). The English stops at the same point with an ellipsis; the next section picks up with the believers being drawn into the observance of the law.
‘μᾶλλον χρῆσαι’ (1 Corinthians 7:21) is kept as ‘rather make use of it’. Cyril’s comment (‘the yoke is not without gain’) shows he takes ‘it’ to mean the state of slavery, not the chance of freedom.

‘ἔσται ἂν ἅπασιν … σώζηται τὸ ἐλεύθερον’: ἔσται with ἂν and a subjunctive is read as ἔστ’ ἄν (‘so long as’), which the subjunctive requires: ‘so long as freedom is kept for all alike’. ‘ἀδικήσει δὲ τὸ σύμπαν οὐδέν’ is ‘will do no wrong at all’, with τὸ σύμπαν adverbial.

‘ὠφελουμένους Χριστῷ’ is rendered as printed (‘helped by him’). The following lines (‘who owe their own life to the One who purchased them’) suggest the reading ὀφειλομένους (‘owed to Christ’) may be original; not adopted without a second witness.
‘μυσταγωγός’ (Paul) is rendered ‘the guide into the mysteries’.
The PG sub-heading ‘ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΚ ΤΟΥ Δ ΤΟΜΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΠΡΟΣ ΚΟΡΙΝΘΙΟΥΣ ΚΥΡΙΛΛΟΥ’ is kept as its own short paragraph.
Isaiah 24:2 in context describes judgment falling on all ranks alike; Cyril reads it as the equality of the life to come. Translated as he uses it.

title: Food Offered to Idols and the Weak Conscience
english: …the believers into the observance of the law. These people pour the venom of the ancient deceit into the souls of the simpler; they persuade them to keep days and months (compare Galatians 4:10), they practice what is called self-made religion (compare Colossians 2:23), and they advise others to choose to fulfill it.

Since, then, he says, you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 7:23), and were ransomed “not with perishable things, with silver or gold,” but rather “with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19), let us rather be subject to his laws.

“Now concerning food offered to idols, we know that we all have knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8:1). The believers at Corinth were convinced that God is by nature one and only, and that idols are not gods. They laughed at those who sacrificed to them, saying that meat offered in sacrifice is nothing at all, and they ate it without distinction, reckoning that no defilement came from it. But they caused the weak to stumble, those who thought they gave no offense to God if they honored the feasts of the idols. For this reason Paul puts a stop to these feasts, wishing the believers to be single-minded, worshiping the all-holy God alone.

“We know that there is no idol in the world” (1 Corinthians 8:4). For those who do not know the idols at all, or who know precisely that they are mere wood and stone, there is no idol in the world, for they do not count them worth any account at all. Thinking in this way, they believe in one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and in one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6).

He has the glory of the lordship of God the Father; and, as the One begotten of him, he has the pre-eminence of the One who begot him, since he exists, and is understood to be, God in his own nature, and not by that participation in the Spirit by which many have been called gods and lords. This knowledge few possess.

“As there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5). It is by being counted worthy of a share in the Holy Spirit that many have been called gods and lords; and this mystical knowledge few possess. For unbelievers still think there are many gods, and some even of those who have believed in Christ do not wholly depart from the customs of idolatry.

“But some, being conscious of the idol until now, eat it as food offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled” (1 Corinthians 8:7). Some of those who have believed in Christ have not wholly turned away from idolatry, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. For out of a weak soul they perhaps even think it benefits them to be purified by sharing in sacred sacrifices, and to make a meal of the sacrificial meat. But the weak must be led on by spiritual teaching, not by eating without distinction and reclining at table with unbelievers.

“But take care that this right of yours does not become a stumbling block to the weak” (1 Corinthians 8:9). By being indifferent about eating sacrificial meat and reclining with unbelievers in the temples, they made the display of their own firmness an occasion of stumbling for some. For we must not use the right that faith gives in every case, nor out of season and without discernment; rather, it would be fitting for everything to be done by us in a seemly way (compare 1 Corinthians 14:40).

“Thus, sinning against the brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:12). By causing the brothers to stumble we shall offend against Christ himself, who died for the salvation of us all; and what wrong could weigh as much as that? For “the weak man is destroyed by your knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8:11); our good has become sin, the firmness of faith a stumbling block to the brothers, and knowledge a pit.

It is a very grievous thing, for it all but amounts to leaping on the weaknesses of the brothers, instead of taking pains to strengthen their weak conscience. For we must “not put a stumbling block or an occasion of falling before a brother” (Romans 14:13), keeping in mind what is…

title: Israel’s Fall in the Wilderness
english: …written: “Do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels always behold the face of the Father” (Matthew 18:10). How then is it not very grievous that we should be accused even by the holy angels themselves, as those who all but leap on the weaknesses of the brothers, and do not rather take pains to strengthen their weak conscience?
Tome 4, Discourse 3.

“I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud” (1 Corinthians 10:1). Having charged those who supposedly have perfect knowledge not to eat sacrificial meat, Paul now tries to persuade them, from what befell the people of old, that the practice is not profitable but rather dangerous, and that it is not without harm to rush in among those accustomed to doing wrong. For it carries one off to do what is not lawful, since the human mind is easily shaken, little by little, toward what is not fitting.

So he takes no unlovely image of the matter, indeed a very close likeness: what happened in the wilderness to those of the blood of Israel. And he shows very forcefully that wanting to live with unbelievers would not be without harm even for those who stand firm.

What he says is this: those who had been freed from slavery were made perfect through the cloud in the sea, with the cloud hanging over them in their midst and Moses acting as mediator (compare 1 Corinthians 10:2). They ate the bread from heaven; they drank the life-giving drink; for Christ gave them drink, being himself the rock (compare 1 Corinthians 10:3–4). For he is unbreakable as God, even though he willingly suffered the assault of death. We say that such things are prefigurings of a spiritual reality.

And what happened to the people of old after this? In what way did they stumble? They were defiled at Shittim, they served idols, they were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; Psalm 106:28). See, then, how those baptized in the cloud and in the sea, though they had eaten the bread from heaven and drunk the spiritual drink, became entangled with the idolaters. Because they shared meals with them and touched the table of the idols, they were at once easily carried away and slid into apostasy, and they danced with women: “And the people who understood were entangled with a prostitute,” in the words of the prophet (Hosea 4:14). For this is what is meant by “they rose up to play” (1 Corinthians 10:7).

So it is dangerous to live in the company of the wicked and the unbelieving. Indeed Solomon said somewhere, “He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be known” (Proverbs 13:20).

For we too, before our faith in Christ, were yoked under the greed of the demons and were slaves to the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, to Satan, the author of evil. We toiled for him in vain, standing in the works of the flesh as in clay and brickmaking (compare Exodus 1:14). But “the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6), rescued us too. He brought us too across the surge of this present life, as across a kind of sea, and made us perfect through holy baptism.

For he is the cloud from above, the spiritual cloud, which supplies living water to those who love it; and the living water is the Spirit. Indeed Christ said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). And the inspired evangelist, making the saying plain, at once added to the words about it, “Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39).
We too have eaten the truly life-giving bread, we have drunk the spiritual drink, just as they drank the water from the rock; and the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), who for us too…
